When Ali grew too weak to walk, he still dragged himself to the office, and his only reply to their mockery was his quiet belief in his daughter's promise and in the compass of a father's heart. The staff's laughter is the story's indictment: a lonely old man's entire world was a daily pilgrimage, and the world answered it with derision.

entries.prompt: What happened on Ali's last visit to the post office, and what effect did it have on the postmaster?
entries.answer: On his last visit, Ali was gravely ill, barely able to walk, and knew he would not live long. He came for the last time, and instead of asking about his letter he made a simple request: that the postmaster keep the letter safe when it came and hand it to him personally, since he trusted no one else in the office. The postmaster, irritated by the old man's persistence, refused to commit himself to any promise. Before leaving, Ali looked at him steadily and said he would come again no more — and something in his tone shook the postmaster, who felt a sudden, nameless chill and could not afterwards get the old man out of his mind. Days later Ali died alone. When the postmaster's own daughter fell ill and sent him a letter, the memory of Ali's face returned like a wound: he understood at last what the old man had suffered, and in remorse he searched the office until he found the letter for Ali that had arrived after Ali's death and lain unclaimed ever since.

entries.prompt: Value question: What does the story teach us about how we should treat the lonely and the aged?
entries.answer: The story teaches that the lonely and the aged ask the world for very little, and the world owes them kindness. Ali asked for nothing but a seat and a promise — yet the clerks mocked his daily pilgrimage and the postmaster dismissed him as a nuisance. The story's lesson is twofold. First, we must never judge another's grief by our own experience: what looked like a foolish obsession was the entire content of an old man's heart, and the postmaster could not understand it until his own daughter's letter taught him in a day what Ali had lived for years. Second, compassion is a duty of time and attention: a few kind words, a promise honoured, would have cost the postmaster nothing and meant everything to Ali. The story ends with the postmaster waiting with Ali's lamp — the lesson finally learned, but too late for the one who needed it. Kindness must be offered while it can still be received.

entries.prompt: Why is the story titled "The Letter"? What role does the letter play?
entries.answer: The letter is the story's central object and symbol. For Ali it is everything: the promised proof of his daughter's love, the one thing that would make his waiting worthwhile. For years he waits for it, and its absence defines his life — hope and its slow dying. The letter's role is also ironic: it arrives at last only after Ali's death, and lies unclaimed in the office while the clerks forget him. Yet the letter's greatest work is done after its arrival: when the postmaster, moved by his own daughter's letter, finds Ali's letter at last, it becomes the instrument of his awakening. It carries the love Ali never received and the lesson the postmaster finally learns — that a letter is not paper and ink but a message between hearts, and that the post office, keeper of such messages, failed its truest customer. The title thus points to both the lost letter of a father and the found lesson of a postmaster.

entries.prompt: How does the postmaster change by the end of the story?
entries.answer: The postmaster changes from indifference to compassion, and the story traces that change as a quiet conversion. At first he is a busy, self-important official who treats Ali as a nuisance, refuses his request and dismisses his faith. But Ali's last words — "I shall come again no more" — leave a chill on him that he cannot shake, and when Ali dies the memory lingers. The true turning point is his own suffering: his daughter falls ill and writes to him, and in holding her letter he feels for the first time the love and fear that drove Ali to the post office every day. In a flood of remorse he searches out Ali's unclaimed letter and, that evening, takes Ali's lamp and waits at the window himself — hoping, as Ali had hoped, for a letter that may never come. The postmaster has become what Ali was: a waiting heart. The story suggests that we understand others' grief only by tasting it, and that it is never too late — though often too late for the person who needed us.

entries.prompt: Part 1 — The meeting by the roadside
entries.answer: The narrator and his friend were driving through the foothills of the Alps when they saw a ruined farmhouse and, beside it, two boys selling wild strawberries. The boys, Nicola and Jacopo, were shabby in dress, with sunburnt faces and honest, cheerful eyes. The narrator bought a basket and was struck by their politeness and their eagerness to please. They were brothers, about twelve and thirteen, and although the narrator and his friend were tourists, the boys treated them with a courtesy that seemed to belong to another age.

entries.prompt: Part 2 — The boys in Verona
entries.answer: Later, in Verona, the narrator met the two boys again in the public square. He learned that they did a dozen odd jobs: they ran errands, sold fruits, polished shoes, drove a taxi and even acted as tourist guides, and they spoke of their work with pride, never complaining. The narrator grew interested in the industrious pair and began to watch them with admiration, struck by their quiet diligence and the way they seemed to be saving every coin they earned.

entries.prompt: Part 3 — The night journey
entries.answer: One evening, the narrator saw Nicola and Jacopo waiting near the theatre and offered them a lift. They asked him to drive them to a village outside Verona, telling him they had an errand. He drove them there — a journey that, as they later said, took them several times a week. The narrator did not ask questions, but his curiosity grew as the boys thanked him and hurried away towards a large, forbidding building.

entries.prompt: Part 4 — The secret and the lesson
entries.answer: The narrator finally discovered the truth: the two "little gentlemen" were visiting their sister Lucia, who was in hospital with tuberculosis of the spine. Her cure needed expensive treatment by a specialist in Padua, which the state could not provide, and the two boys were working day and night to pay for it. The narrator realised that his "protégés" were heroes: poor, orphaned by the war, yet brave, honest and selfless in their love for their sister. He understood then that the title "two gentlemen" belonged to them in the truest sense — for gentility, he learned, is a quality of the heart, not of class or circumstance.

entries.prompt: True gentility lies in character
entries.answer: The story's central theme is that true gentility has nothing to do with wealth or rank. Nicola and Jacopo are poor, shabby boys doing menial jobs, yet they are called "gentlemen" because of their honesty, courage, courtesy and selfless love. The narrator, who at first thinks of the boys with condescension, learns that the noblest qualities — hard work, loyalty and sacrifice — can shine in the humblest lives. The title is the story's thesis: a gentleman is made by character, not class.

entries.prompt: Sacrifice and selfless love
entries.answer: The theme of sacrifice runs through the story. The two boys give up their childhood — play, comfort and rest — to earn money for their sister's treatment. They endure cold, hunger and hardship without a word of complaint, spending their earnings on Lucia's cure rather than on themselves. Their love is entirely selfless: they work "like men" and behave "like boys", and every rupee they earn is for their sister. The story celebrates this quiet heroism of the poor.

entries.prompt: The scars of war
entries.answer: The story is set against the ruins of the Second World War. The boys have lost their home, their father (killed in the war) and their mother (died in an early bomb raid), and their sister's illness is itself a legacy of hardship. Yet the brothers do not beg or complain; they rebuild their lives with dignity and work. The theme shows that war destroys, but the human spirit — courage, hope and love — can survive even its ruins.

entries.prompt: Nicola
entries.answer: Nicola, the elder brother, is about thirteen years old. He is the steady, responsible one — mature beyond his years, doing the hardest work (shoeshining, errands, taxi driving) and managing the family's affairs. He is polite and composed, and when the narrator offers help, Nicola politely refuses, insisting they do not need it. His quiet dignity, his endurance and his devotion to his sister make him one of the story's two "gentlemen".

entries.prompt: Jacopo
entries.answer: Jacopo, the younger brother, is about twelve. He is more boyish than Nicola — when the narrator offers him a ride, he jumps in gleefully and talks happily — yet he shares his brother's industry and devotion. He sells fruits, polishes shoes and guides tourists with the same cheerful earnestness. His youthful spirit, preserved even under hardship, makes his sacrifice all the more moving: a child who still smiles while working like a man.

entries.prompt: The narrator
entries.answer: The narrator is a writer touring Italy after the war, a man of means who at first regards the boys with amused patronage — he calls them his "protégés" and feels he is doing them a favour. His discovery of the truth transforms him: he realises that the boys he pitied were far nobler than he, and that his condescension was misplaced. He represents the reader — learning that true gentility is measured by the heart. His final vision of the two brothers "whole and healed" in the future gives the story its hope.

entries.prompt: Lucia
entries.answer: Lucia is the boys' sister, ill with tuberculosis of the spine, who lies in a hospital outside Verona. She never appears directly in the action — we know her only through her brothers' devotion. Her treatment by a specialist in Padua is the object of all their labour, and the narrator learns her name and her illness on the night he follows Nicola to the hospital. She is the invisible centre of the story: the living reason for the boys' sacrifice, and the symbol of everything worth working for.

entries.prompt: Hard work and self-respect
entries.answer: The story teaches the dignity of honest labour. The two boys work at a dozen humble jobs — shining shoes, selling fruits, running errands — and never complain or beg. They accept help only on their own terms and preserve their self-respect. The value lesson: honest work, however small, is noble, and poverty is no shame; laziness and self-pity are.

entries.prompt: Love and sacrifice for family
entries.answer: The boys' devotion to their sister is the story's great value lesson. They sacrifice their own childhood and comfort so that Lucia can be cured, and they do it secretly, without seeking praise or pity. The lesson: family love is a duty and a joy, and sacrifice for those we love ennobles the giver. True gentility, the story insists, is measured by what we give, not what we have.

entries.prompt: Where did the narrator first meet the two boys?
entries.answer: He met them beside a ruined farmhouse in the foothills of the Alps, where they were selling wild strawberries.

entries.prompt: What were the names of the two boys?
entries.answer: Nicola and Jacopo, brothers of about thirteen and twelve years of age.

entries.prompt: What jobs did the boys do in Verona?
entries.answer: They ran errands, sold fruits, polished shoes, drove a taxi and acted as tourist guides.

entries.prompt: Why did the boys ask the narrator to drive them to the village?
entries.answer: They said they had an errand; in truth they went to visit their sick sister Lucia in hospital.

entries.prompt: Who was Lucia and what was her illness?
entries.answer: Lucia was the boys' sister, who was suffering from tuberculosis of the spine.

entries.prompt: Why did the boys work so hard?
entries.answer: To pay for the expensive treatment of their sister by a specialist in Padua, which the state could not provide.

entries.prompt: How did the boys lose their parents?
entries.answer: Their father was killed in the war and their mother died in an early bomb raid; their home was also destroyed.

entries.prompt: Why are the boys called "gentlemen"?
entries.answer: Because of their courage, honesty, courtesy and selfless love — true gentility lies in character, not class.

entries.prompt: Describe the character of Nicola and Jacopo. What makes them "gentlemen"?
entries.answer: Nicola and Jacopo are brothers, about thirteen and twelve, who have lost their home and parents to the war. Nicola is the responsible elder — composed, steady and mature, doing the hardest work; Jacopo is the younger, more boyish and cheerful, yet equally industrious. Together they do a dozen humble jobs — shining shoes, selling fruits, running errands, driving a taxi, guiding tourists — always polite, never complaining. What makes them "gentlemen" is not their clothes or station but their character: their honesty (they refuse charity and pay their own way), their courage (they bear their orphanhood and poverty with dignity), and above all their selfless love for their sister, for whose cure they sacrifice their own childhood, working "like men" while still boys. The narrator learns that gentility is a quality of the heart.

entries.prompt: What did the narrator discover on the night he followed Nicola?
entries.answer: One evening the narrator offered the boys a lift and they asked him to drive them to a village outside Verona, saying they had an errand. Curious, he drove them and watched as they hurried towards a large building. He asked a woman who worked there who the boys visited, and learned the truth: they came to see their sister Lucia, who was ill with tuberculosis of the spine and lay in a hospital there. Her cure required expensive treatment by a specialist in Padua, which the state did not cover, and the two boys were working day and night to pay for it. The narrator, who had thought of them as poor but cheerful boys, was deeply moved: he realised they had been coming this way several times a week, and that their cheerfulness and industry were really a quiet act of heroism. That night he understood why he had grown to love them — they were the bravest boys he had ever known.

entries.prompt: Value question: What does the story teach us about the meaning of true nobility?
entries.answer: The story teaches that true nobility lies in character, not in birth, wealth or status. The two boys are poor, shabby and orphaned; their jobs are the humblest in the town. Yet they possess the qualities we call noble: honesty (they refuse the narrator's help with quiet dignity), industry (they work at a dozen trades without complaint), courage (they face war, poverty and illness with unbroken spirits) and above all selfless love — they give up their childhood so that their sister may live. The narrator, a man of means who at first patronises them, is the story's lesson in humility: he learns that he, not the boys, was the poorer one in spirit. The value we take away is that gentility is earned by the heart — by how much we give, how hard we work and how loyally we love — and that the humblest person can be the greatest gentleman.

entries.prompt: How does the story use its setting to deepen its themes?
entries.answer: The story is set in Italy just after the Second World War, and its setting is not decoration but meaning. The ruined farmhouse by the roadside, the shabby clothes of the boys, the market work of Verona — all speak of a country and a people scarred by war. The boys are themselves victims of the war: their father was killed, their mother died in a bomb raid, their home was destroyed, and their sister's illness is part of the suffering the war left behind. Yet the setting also shows resilience: life goes on — strawberries are sold, shoes are polished, taxis run, and two boys rebuild a future out of ruins. The contrast between the ruined landscape and the boys' unbroken hope deepens the theme of human courage, and the hospital outside Verona, where Lucia lies, gives the setting its centre: a place of suffering that the boys' love is fighting to transform into healing.

entries.prompt: Why does the narrator say he had been "fooled" by the boys? What does this reveal?
entries.answer: The narrator says he had been fooled because he had believed Nicola and Jacopo were simply cheerful, hardworking boys who enjoyed their independence — perhaps saving money for some boyish dream. He had no idea that they were working day and night to pay for their sister's treatment, or that their evening errands took them to her hospital bedside several times a week. His discovery reveals two things. First, it shows the boys' nobility: they carried their burden in total secrecy, never asking for pity or help, and their cheerfulness was a brave disguise. Second, it reveals the narrator's own growth: he had looked at the boys with kindly condescension, calling them his protégés, and now he understands that they were never his dependents — he had misjudged them because he measured their worth by their shabby clothes and humble work. His "fooling" teaches him, and us, to look past appearances to the true measure of a person.

entries.prompt: Part 1 — The second-hand computer
entries.answer: The narrator, a schoolboy, was delighted when his family bought a second-hand 486 computer with a 14-inch monitor from a computer shop. Along with it came a crate of games. Exploring the machine, he found the previous owner had left files on the hard disk — and among them, a game unlike any other. What began as an ordinary purchase would draw him into the strangest adventure of his life: the rescue of a boy trapped inside the machine.

entries.prompt: Part 2 — The games and the stranger
entries.answer: As the narrator played game after game — a dragon quest, a wartime flying game, a space battle, a tennis championship — a strange character kept appearing: a boy named Sebastian Shultz, who was not part of any of the games. Each time, Sebastian pleaded for help, saying he was trapped and that only the narrator could save him. Puzzled and intrigued, the narrator kept playing, following the clues Sebastian left, and in each game he managed to rescue Sebastian from the perils the game threw at him — dragons, enemy planes, alien ships and a ruthless opponent.

entries.prompt: Part 3 — Sebastian's story
entries.answer: Piece by piece, Sebastian told his story: he was the son of Professor Shultz, a scientist who had built a virtual reality system — a helmet that let a player's mind enter the games themselves. During an experiment, Sebastian's mind had been caught in the system, and when the computer was sold and the files scattered, he was left trapped in the game data, waiting for someone to play through and free him. The narrator realised that his "games" were in fact a rescue mission — and that he was the only one who could finish it.

entries.prompt: Part 4 — The rescue and the truth
entries.answer: In the final game, following Sebastian's instructions exactly, the narrator defeated the game and freed him. Sebastian's grateful face vanished from the screen, and his message was simple: thank you. Days later, the narrator read in the newspaper that Sebastian Shultz — a boy who had been in a coma for years after a car accident — had unexpectedly woken up and was recovering, his father Professor Shultz at his bedside. The narrator smiled: he had been playing for real. What had seemed a virtual world had reached across into the real one — and he had saved a real boy.

entries.prompt: The blurring of virtual and real
entries.answer: The story's central theme is the mysterious border between the virtual and the real. What seems to be a set of computer games is in fact a lifeline to a real boy in a coma: his mind lives inside the game data, and the narrator's play is real rescue. The story explores how technology can connect people across impossible distances — between a machine and a hospital bed — and asks whether the "virtual" is ever truly separate from our lives. It is a story of technology's power, both to trap and to free.

entries.prompt: Persistence, patience and compassion
entries.answer: The narrator succeeds not by luck but by persistence: he plays each game again and again, follows Sebastian's instructions with patience, and refuses to give up when the games defeat him. His compassion matters as much as his skill — he believes in a stranger he has never met and keeps faith with him across levels and worlds. The theme celebrates the quiet virtues of perseverance and kindness: the boy who won a championship in the game was really the boy who refused to abandon another boy in need.

entries.prompt: Technology and human connection
entries.answer: The story is also about what technology can do for love. Professor Shultz built the virtual reality system to reach his son, using games to exercise and stimulate Sebastian's mind while his body lay in a coma; the narrator, a total stranger, completes the task by playing. The theme suggests that machines are never more than tools — the real magic is in the human beings who use them with hope and care. Father and stranger, miles and machines apart, unite across the virtual world to save one boy.

entries.prompt: The narrator
entries.answer: The narrator is an ordinary schoolboy with a new second-hand computer and a love of games. He is curious, observant and unshakably persistent: where another player might dismiss Sebastian as a game glitch, he listens, believes and keeps playing until the task is done. His compassion is his defining trait — he takes on the rescue of a stranger he has never met and never doubts that Sebastian is real. He is the reader's stand-in: an ordinary boy who, by caring and persevering, becomes a hero in the only way that matters.

entries.prompt: Sebastian Shultz
entries.answer: Sebastian is the genius boy trapped inside the games — the son of Professor Shultz, inventor of the virtual reality helmet. In every game world he appears as a character in need: a victim of dragons, of war, of space battles, of a merciless tennis opponent. His messages grow more urgent as the story unfolds, and his story — of a mind caught in an experiment and left behind when the computer was sold — is the story's mystery. His grateful farewell and his recovery in the real world confirm what the narrator always believed: Sebastian was always real, and he was always worth saving.

entries.prompt: Professor Shultz
entries.answer: Professor Shultz is Sebastian's father and the creator of the virtual reality system. He appears only in Sebastian's account and in the closing newspaper report, yet he is the story's emotional source: a scientist who used his own invention to fight for his son, building games designed to reach and heal Sebastian's injured mind. His dedication — years of patient work, games crafted as therapy — is the love that makes the whole rescue possible. His image, waiting at his recovered son's bedside, closes the story on a note of hope: science and love, working together.

entries.prompt: The narrator's parents
entries.answer: The narrator's parents are the story's voices of ordinary reality. They buy the computer, warn against too much screen time, and worry about his hours of play — never suspecting that their son is on a life-or-death mission. Their gentle scepticism ("it's only a game") sets up the story's wonder: when the news arrives that a boy has woken from a coma, the narrator alone knows what really happened. They represent the everyday world that cannot see the magic in the machine — and the story delights in proving them wrong.

entries.prompt: Persistence pays — never give up
entries.answer: The narrator wins his games only by replaying, learning and refusing to quit, and Sebastian is saved because someone kept going. The value lesson: difficult tasks — games, studies, problems — are mastered by patience and repeated effort, not by luck. The boy who persisted through every level is the boy who saved a life.

entries.prompt: Compassion for strangers; use technology for good
entries.answer: The narrator helps someone he has never met, purely because help was asked. The value lesson is twofold: first, kindness should not depend on knowing the person — a stranger's need is reason enough to act; second, technology, for all its dangers, is a tool for good when guided by care and love — as Professor Shultz's games and the narrator's play both prove.

entries.prompt: Suspense and mystery structure
entries.answer: The story is built like a mystery: each game ends with a new clue, each of Sebastian's messages raises new questions, and the truth — that the games are therapy and the game character a real boy — is revealed only in layers. The structure keeps the reader playing alongside the narrator, and the final newspaper report delivers the satisfying click of the last puzzle piece.

entries.prompt: Foreshadowing
entries.answer: The story plants careful hints of its final revelation: Sebastian's strange persistence across games, his knowledge of the narrator's score, his urgency, and his father's mysterious "experiment". Each detail, odd in the moment, is explained by the ending — the reader looks back and sees the clues everywhere. This device makes the twist feel earned rather than sudden.

entries.prompt: Dramatic irony
entries.answer: The story is rich in dramatic irony: the parents see only games, the shopkeeper sees only a sale, and even the reader at first sees only play — while the truth, that a boy's life depends on the game, is gradually revealed. When the narrator finally reads the newspaper, the irony is complete: he alone knows that the "miracle" recovery was, in part, his own doing.

entries.prompt: Symbolism of the games
entries.answer: Each game world symbolises a stage of Sebastian's struggle: dragons and wars are the perils of his trapped mind; the championship tennis match is the final test of his recovery. The games are not entertainment but trials — therapy in code — and the narrator's victories are milestones of healing. The symbolism deepens the story's wonder: play, which seems the most frivolous of activities, becomes the instrument of a miracle.

entries.prompt: What did the narrator's family buy at the start of the story?
entries.answer: A second-hand 486 computer with a 14-inch monitor, together with a crate of games.

entries.prompt: Who was Sebastian Shultz?
entries.answer: The son of Professor Shultz, a boy whose mind was trapped inside the computer's game data.

entries.prompt: How did Sebastian appear in the games?
entries.answer: He appeared as a character in each game, pleading with the narrator to rescue him.

entries.prompt: What had Professor Shultz invented?
entries.answer: A virtual reality system — a helmet that let a player's mind enter the games themselves.

entries.prompt: How had Sebastian's mind become trapped?
entries.answer: During an experiment with his father's virtual reality system, his mind was caught in the game data, and when the computer was sold he was left behind.

entries.prompt: How did the narrator free Sebastian?
entries.answer: By completing every game and following Sebastian's instructions, rescuing him in each one until he was finally set free.

entries.prompt: What did the newspaper report at the end of the story?
entries.answer: That Sebastian Shultz, a boy who had been in a coma after a car accident, had woken up and was recovering with his father at his bedside.

entries.prompt: What did the narrator realise at the end?
entries.answer: That his virtual games had been real — he had saved a real boy, and the "game" was truly a rescue.

entries.prompt: Describe the narrator's encounters with Sebastian in the games.
entries.answer: Game after game, the narrator met a character who had no business being there: Sebastian Shultz. In the dragon quest, he was a frightened figure among the perils of the medieval world; in the wartime flying game, he was a pilot in trouble; in the space battle, a lost soul among alien ships; and in the tennis championship, a player at the mercy of a ruthless opponent. In every encounter Sebastian spoke to the narrator directly, telling him he was trapped and begging for help, and each time the narrator acted: he fought the dragon, saved the pilot, escaped the aliens and beat the opponent. What puzzled him was that Sebastian never seemed to belong to the game — his words were not part of the program. Only later did the narrator understand that Sebastian's mind was genuinely inside the data, and that every game was one more piece of the prison he had to unlock.

entries.prompt: How did the narrator come to understand Sebastian's story?
entries.answer: The narrator pieced Sebastian's story together from the messages he left in each game. Sebastian told him that he was the son of Professor Shultz, a scientist who had built a virtual reality system — a helmet that could put a player's mind directly inside a computer game. During an experiment, Sebastian's mind had been caught in the system and could not get out. Then the computer was sold, its files were scattered, and Sebastian was left trapped in the game data, cut off from the real world. He had been waiting for someone — anyone — who would play the games to the end and follow his instructions, because his freedom was coded into the games themselves. The narrator now understood why Sebastian kept appearing across such different worlds: each game held a part of him, and only a complete play-through could set him free.

entries.prompt: Value question: What does the story teach us about persistence and compassion?
entries.answer: The story teaches that persistence and compassion can achieve what seems impossible. The narrator meets a stranger in a game and chooses to believe him, to keep playing when the levels defeat him, and to follow instructions that make no sense to anyone else. His patience is not rewarded by the game's score but by something infinitely better: a boy's life. The value lesson is that we should not give up on difficult tasks — mastery comes from repeated effort, and the difference between winning and losing is often simply continuing. It also teaches that compassion does not require acquaintance: the narrator helps Sebastian because help was needed, not because he knew him. And it warns against dismissing the strange or the inexplicable too quickly — the "game glitch" was a cry for help. In a world of screens and machines, the story insists, the most important thing is still the human heart that plays, cares and refuses to quit.

entries.prompt: How does the story blur the line between the virtual and the real world?
entries.answer: The story deliberately dissolves the boundary between virtual and real. On the surface, the narrator is playing ordinary computer games — fantasy, war, space, sport — but inside those games lives a real boy, and the narrator's play is a genuine rescue. The virtual reality helmet, designed to put a mind inside a machine, is the bridge: Sebastian's consciousness exists in the game data exactly as it would in a body, and his suffering is real suffering. The games are in fact therapy — Professor Shultz's loving design to exercise his son's injured mind — so the "virtual" worlds are really the instruments of a real recovery. The final newspaper report completes the blur: the miracle in a hospital ward and the boy at a computer screen are the same story. The story's wonder is precisely this — that in an age of screens, the deepest realities can still pass through them, and a game can carry a life.

entries.prompt: Do you think the narrator was "virtually" a hero, or a real one? Give reasons.
entries.answer: The narrator was a real hero in every sense, though his heroism looked virtual. He never left his room, never saw Sebastian, never spoke to him — his entire adventure was played on a screen. Yet his actions had real consequences: he completed the games that freed a trapped mind, and the boy in the newspaper, awake and recovering, was saved because an unknown player refused to stop. Heroism is measured by effect, not by spectacle: the narrator risked nothing physically, but he gave his time, his patience and his belief. He trusted a voice in a machine when he might have shrugged it off as a glitch; he kept faith when the games defeated him; he finished what Sebastian's father had begun. In the end, the word "virtually" in the title carries the story's irony: nothing about the rescue was virtual at all. The narrator saved a real boy, and that makes him a real hero.
